title: Wavelet Flow Matching for Multi-Scale Physics Emulation
claim: Generative emulation can be trained by applying optimal-transport flow matching jointly across all wavelet scales through one shared conditioned network.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right data flow, legend inset top-left, loss box bottom-right
description: A single-panel training-pipeline diagram with a rounded legend box at top-left (concatenation circle, learnable-embedding wave icon, DWT hexagon). On the left, the next-state field x^{t+1} goes through a DWT block to give multi-scale wavelet tiles w_j^{t+1}. Gaussian noise tiles ε_j ~ N(0, I) sit below. Both feed a gray 'Multi-scale Optimal Transport Paths' box. Dashed arrows lead from it to noisy interpolated wavelet tiles w_j^τ. The current state x^t also goes through a DWT, and the result is concatenated with w_j^τ to form z_j^τ. A purple box holds the velocity-prediction U-Net û_j = u_θ(z, τ, κ, past frames). It also receives PDE constants κ, τ and past frames x^{t-l} through embedding icons. The output goes to a blue dashed loss box ℓ_j(θ) = E||û_j − u_j||². Red/blue fluid-field images carry the eye first.
caption: Illustration of the Wavelet Flow Matching architecture. During training, Gaussian noise is sampled to match the shape of wavelet coefficients at each scale. OT-CFM interpolation is applied between the next-state wavelet coefficients \(w_j^{t+1}\) and noise at every scale with a shared interpolation time \(\tau\), yielding \(J\) per-scale flows that are coupled through the shared U-Net. The velocity-predicting U-Net \(u_{\theta}\) (purple box) is conditioned on the interpolation step \(\tau\), the channel-wise concatenation $z_j^{\tau}$ of \(w_j^{\tau}\) and the current-state coefficients \(w_j^{t}\), PDE constants \(\kappa\), and embedding of past $L$ frames. The illustration of $u_{\theta}$ is shown in Figure [ref].
abstract: Accurate emulation of multi-scale physical systems governed by PDEs demands models that remain stable over long autoregressive rollouts while preserving fine-scale structures. Deterministic emulators produce overly smoothed predictions, while generative approaches better capture details but are costly. Latent-space generative models have emerged as a compromise but with the additional cost of separately pre-trained autoencoders. We propose Wavelet Flow Matching (WFM), a generative emulator that overcomes current trade-offs between cost and skill by performing optimal-transport flow matching directly in the multi-scale wavelet space. Rather than learning a latent compression, WFM leverages the hierarchical structure of a U-Net to jointly predict the transport velocities of a prescribed, lossless wavelet representation. On three challenging systems of chaotic fluid dynamics, WFM achieves superior spectral coherence and competitive or better long-horizon accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models. Our results position the wavelet space as an effective training-free representation for generative emulation of complex physical dynamics.
